# MCP Tool Design: Why Your AI Agent Is Failing (And How to Fix It)

#mcp #ai #rust #llm

## The Reports of MCP's Death Have Been Greatly Exaggerated

Scroll through developer forums in early 2026, and you'll find a recurring theme: MCP is dead. The takes range from dismissive ("just a fad") to resigned ("we tried it, our agents kept failing"). And the frustrations behind them are real. Teams are building MCP servers with 50+ tools, watching their agents stumble through tool selection, and concluding that the protocol itself is broken. [...] 1. The Capability Square drives everything. Good tool design requires balancing four parties: what the LLM can do (interpret intent, select tools), what the server should do (precise computation, data access), what the business analyst knows at design time (which capabilities matter, how to describe them, which user persona they serve), and what the business user brings at runtime (the actual request and its business context). When any corner is weak, task completion suffers.
2. Design for outcomes, not operations. One tool per user goal, not one tool per API endpoint. The customer asking "where's my order?" wants a tracking link, not three chained API calls. Move orchestration complexity into the server, where it runs deterministically. [...] This iterative loop is where MCP shines compared to direct API integration. Changing a tool's name, description, or input schema is a server-side change, with no client updates, no SDK version bumps, no breaking changes propagated to consumers. The MCP protocol decouples tool discovery from tool invocation, so the LLM rediscovers the improved schema on the next connection. This makes the feedback cycle fast: observe failures, update the tool design, deploy, and measure again. Teams that treat tool design as a one-time exercise miss the biggest advantage of having MCP in the middle. You should put effort into designing the MCP server correctly, as "You never get a second chance to make a first impression." ## AI Agents

# Your AI Agent Has 150 Tools and Can’t Do Anything Right

## I gave my agent every MCP server I could find. It got slower, dumber, and more expensive. Then a single markdown file fixed it.

Deval Shah

--

Listen

Share

Cover Image

Last Tuesday at 2 AM, I watched my agent burn through $4 in API calls trying to create a pull request. It had access to the GitHub MCP server — all 30 tools, perfectly configured.

It picked the wrong endpoint three times, hallucinated a nonexistent parameter, and then apologized and started over.

I’d been building with AI agents for over a year. I had the setup everyone recommends: five MCP servers, 150 tool definitions, a beautiful architecture diagram I was quietly proud of. [...] I started noticing a pattern. The more tools I gave my agent, the worse it performed. More hallucinations. Longer response times. Higher costs. It would pick a sophisticated MCP tool over a simple one.

A simple command`git push` would have worked fine.

`git push`

Then one night, I tried something different. I deleted the GitHub MCP server and replaced it with a markdown file that said: “You have access to the `gh` CLI. Use it."

`gh`

200 tokens instead of 50,000. A 250x reduction.

The agent got faster. It got cheaper. And weirdly, it got smarter — because it wasn’t drowning in tool definitions anymore. It could actually focus on my task.

I’m not the only one noticing this.

results.content: AI setup much better. I think that MCPs are what we need to make coding agents truly amazing. I also think that we should not design MCPs as mirrors of CLIs or APIs. They're bridges to capabilities agents might need and not or shouldn't be reflections of what we already have. Agents are trying to fulfill user intentions and we should design MCPS to help them with that. MCPS should either provide access to tools and services that the agent cannot already access or they should reflect user intents. The first group is simple. If for example we would like an agent to send a message to Slack, having an MCP that can act as a bridge between that agent and Slack makes a lot of sense. There is maybe probably Slack CLI, but it's not widely adopted and models aren't familiar with it. There is an API [...] in their diversity and specialization. Just as our body has organs optimized for completely different tasks, each MCP server can be purpose-built for specific functions. One might connect to a better service, another to a database, a third to a calendar system, and yet another one to the file system. Some might be simple tools that retrieve information, while others might be complex systems that can perform intricate operations, complicated operations. And here's what's really cool about this. No matter what each MCP server actually does behind the scenes, they all present the same interface to the agent. This standardization means that new capabilities can be added to the AI system simply by connecting new MCP servers without requiring the agent or the brain to learn new communication [...] that your agent can already use it to interact with the cluster. You do not, and I repeat, not need Kubernetes MCP if that MCP is a reflection of cube control. And that part is important. If you're working with Go, agent is more than capable of building a project using Go CLI. So, you get the point, right? I hope so, at least. So, what's the takeaway here? results.title: Turn Your AI Agent into an MCP Server for ChatGPT, Claude & Cursor | Quickchat AI - AI Agents
results.content:
One tool per agent. The server exposes a single tool (you will name it; ours is `ask_orbit`) that takes one string argument, `message`, and returns your agent’s reply. The tool is annotated read-only: it cannot modify anything, on your account or anywhere else.
 Sessions map to conversations. Each MCP session maps to one conversation in your Inbox. A client that keeps its session alive across calls threads follow-ups into that same conversation; many chat apps open a fresh session per question, though, so in practice you will often see each question land as its own conversation. Idle sessions expire after a few hours. [...] The URL is an address, not a secret. The agent id in the URL is the same identifier your website widget exposes publicly. Knowing it is not enough: the visibility toggle is the access control.
 The tool is read-only and scoped to answering. One tool, one string in, one reply out, marked read-only for the calling app. There is no path from the MCP server to your account, settings, Knowledge Base contents or other agents. The worst a caller can do is have a conversation with your agent. [...] ## Introduction

Every tutorial in this series so far has connected a Quickchat AI Agent to something: Telegram, Google Sheets, Discord. This one inverts the direction. Your agent becomes the thing other AIs connect to: a tool that ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor call when their users ask something only your agent knows.

The mechanism is an MCP server, and the setup is deliberately boring: every Quickchat AI Agent already has one, hosted at a URL of the form ` You switch it on, copy the URL, and paste it into the AI app as a connector. That is the whole integration, and it takes no code. Access is private by default: connecting requires signing in with your Quickchat AI account until you decide otherwise.

results.title: AI Agent Portability | Guild.ai
results.content: Model Context Protocol (MCP), originally developed by Anthropic, standardizes how agents connect to external tools, data sources, and memory. MCP is the "USB-C port" for plug-and-play connections between LLMs (or agent frameworks) and external tools, memory stores, or live data.
